comparison: Both evaluate the simulation results comparing response gain and tuning sharpening models (C41-C49, C52, C74). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with clear differentiation between models. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the simulation favors tuning but noting a weakness: 'Direct estimation of baseline responses may have improved the validity of the modelling.'

Both address the weaker PPA results explanation (C38). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED as a reasonable interpretation given PPA's selectivity profile. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED, with no challenges to this interpretation noted.

Both evaluate the V1 findings and explanation (C68-C72, C30). OpenEval finds the explanation SUPPORTED though somewhat speculative. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED, noting the methodological choice of 'transparently overlapping items' has 'some methodological advantages' and implicitly accepting the V1 results.

Both address the core empirical finding that attentional bias depends on target-distractor similarity (C30, C34, C51, C62, C63, C65). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as a well-supported core result. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED, confirming the pattern in both univariate and multivariate analyses, with the editor describing 'convincing data.'

Both evaluate the mechanistic interpretation of tuning sharpening (C53, C54, C66, C67, C78, C83, C84, C81, C82). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED while appropriately acknowledging simulation limitations. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN, noting the study has 'potential to shed mechanistic light' but expressing reservations about baseline estimation affecting modeling validity.

Both evaluate experimental design and stimulus parameters (C5-C15). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with clear justification and sufficient detail for replication. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging methodological strengths including the use of a priori ROIs and both univariate and multivariate analyses.

Both address ROI selection and fMRI methods (C17-C24). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED with appropriate justification and sufficient detail, noting the two-scanner issue as a potential confound. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED with no concerns raised about these methodological aspects.

Both evaluate participant recruitment and sample size (C1-C4, C16). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with adequate power analysis justification and transparent reporting of data loss. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED with no concerns raised about participant numbers.

Both address behavioral performance/detection rate (C26). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as strong evidence of maintained attention. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED with no concerns about behavioral performance.

Both evaluate background literature and motivation (C50, C55-C59). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as well-established background appropriately framing the research question. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED, stating the manuscript 'clearly articulates a core issue in the cognitive neuroscience of attention.'

Both address the characterization of competing models (C60-C61). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as accurate descriptions with appropriate citations. Peer review includes these in broader SUPPORTED evaluation of theoretical framing.

Both evaluate characterization of prior literature (C64, C75, C79-C80). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as accurate with appropriate citations establishing context. Peer review includes these in SUPPORTED evaluation of the theoretical framework.

Both address the mechanistic explanation (C76-C77). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as a well-reasoned inference from the tuning sharpening model. Peer review includes this in broader evaluation but expresses some uncertainty about mechanistic conclusions.

Both address the predictability limitation (C73). OpenEval rates it UNCERTAIN as an appropriate acknowledgment of a limitation that doesn't invalidate core results. Peer review rates the broader theoretical framing SUPPORTED but notes this limitation regarding predictability of distractors.

Both evaluate the acknowledgment of simulation limitations (C81-C82). OpenEval rates it SUPPORTED as an appropriate and transparent discussion strengthening the paper. Peer review's UNCERTAIN rating for mechanistic conclusions implicitly acknowledges these limitations, noting concerns about modeling validity.
